Today if you tell me, go into banking, I am not going to go into banking. She was very fond of classical music. When I met her she looked me in the face and said: ‘there’s something you don’t know about yourself, you are deeper than you think. You are very emotional, I see you with your friends expressing yourselves at a social gathering. But deep down, you are a very serious person’. “One day, she joined me in the preview room, where we played some classical music. At one point, when we were playing some aspects of Mozart’s songs, I got drawn into it, forcing me to go back to play it again. Before I knew what was happening, it stuck,” he told Vanguard. Edochie, however, boasted of having in his archives all the works of Mozart and George Campbell who wrote songs such as “Messiah”, “Saul”, “Solomon” among others. He confessed to placing orders for classical music from abroad, and even urged his friends travelling abroad to buy classical music for him as a gift, instead of shoes, ties and wrist watches. How he wanted to be remembered There are many things to remember Pete Edochie for. His deep baritone voice. His age-long beard. His intimidating look. His danc steps and his father-figure role in Nollywood. But beyond all of these, Ebubedike wanted to be remembered for something far simpler, and far deeper. He wanted to be remembered as a man who brought happiness and joy to many homes in Africa and beyond with his craft. Speaking with Vanguard as he celebrated his 76th birthday in 2023, Edochie opened up on his legacy, honour and fulfilment: “If people feel that my contributions toward the growth of the Nigerian movie industry have affected their lives in one way or the other, it means that posterity would award me good marks. Our industry is very challenging. While you are playing different characters in movies, you are still expected to live up to your billing as a man of honour. “People enjoy me going by their reactions to what I do. It gives me a lot of satisfaction that people think this man knows what he’s doing. If I am remembered as one who injected some life into his audiences in Nigeria and beyond, I feel accomplished,” he said. It was a simple but profound desire from a man whose career spanned more than five decades. For Edochie, acting was not just entertainment. It was a ministry. It was a service. It was a calling to heal homes with laughter, with wisdom, and with stories that mirrored real life. In his own words, all he ever wanted was to bring joy into people’s homes. And by all accounts, that is precisely what he did for more than 50 years, before bowing out of the stage. Landing role of Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s ‘Things Fall Apart’ Pete Edochie did not start his journey as an actor. He started as a broadcaster in 1967 before gaining widespread recognition through his portrayal of Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s celebrated novel, “Things Fall Apart” in the 80s. Recalling how he landed that iconic role in our 2022 interview with him, Edochie said his former colleague, the late G. C. Ugwu, recommended him for the role of Okonkwo. “He was the Zonal Director of NTA in Benin in those days. Engr Ugwu had always watched me in the broadcasting house, and the moment they decided to produce the play, the first person that came to his mind, who would play the role of Okonkwo was me”, he said. He disclosed that he had never read “Things Fall Apart” before the adaptation and his first encounter with the story was through the script. According to him, he auditioned at the University of Nigeria’s Enugu campus. In his account, the production team offered him the role after hearing him read. The performance drew attention beyond Nigeria, and the BBC team travelled to the country to interview him about it. That one role changed African television forever. It made him a household name. It made Okonkwo very popular. And it made Pete Edochie the standard by which every other African actor would be judged. Narrating the story, Edochie agreed that there was always a reflection of the Okonkwo character in most of his roles in movies. “That’s what many people said. When I started in ‘Things Fall Apart’, I was 38 years old. People still call me, “Ebubedike.” Before Chinua Achebe died, he was calling me Ebubedike. He never called me Pete, and we were very close. “Each time people visited him in America then, he would ask after me. Achebe created the character and he felt I interpreted the role excellently. He named me after Okonkwo- Ebube Dike. So, many people still see me and refer to me as an Ebubedike.” He said when the script was handed over to him, he felt it was an opportunity to read the novel since he didn’t have the privilege to do so while he was in school. “I was delighted to read the novel. Before then, I had not read it, I knew nothing about it,” Edochie stated. Ebubedike was not the only actor who auditioned for the iconic role of Okonkwo, but his talent stood him out in the crowd. According to him, “there were other actors who came for the audition held at the main auditorium of the University of Nigeria, Enugu campus. item.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi The sound of gunfire shattered the campaign atmosphere at Uduere, Ughelli North Local Government Area of Delta State, November 23. People who had gathered for a political rally suddenly scrambled for safety. Women ran, campaigners scattered and, in the ensuing chaos, bullets found human targets. By the time the shooting stopped, families had lost loved ones, several people critically wounded and communities plunged into mourning. Among the disturbing details was that six truckloads of policemen had reportedly been deployed to provide security. Former Deputy Senate President, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, put their number at close to 50. Yet, according to accounts from both political camps, the violence escalated despite the robust security presence. The tragedy has since generated competing accusations between the All Progressives Congress, APC, and the National Democratic Congress, NDC. He argued: “The NDC is not being attacked, there are a number of local governments where we have not had any disturbances. The APC in Delta is holding sway, the underdogs in this case are the members of the NDC who are few.” But NDC governorship candidate, Chris Iyovwaye, disagreed, recalling the September incident. “Another thug of APC was caught with an AK-47 and was handed over to the police. To our surprise, he was let off the hook the very next day,” he alleged. On the Asaba attack, he said: “Every time we are exercising our democratic rights, they’re always there to stop us.” Regarding Uduere, Iyovwaye said the party had secured police approval and was promised six truckloads of policemen. “Yet the consequence of that is that four of our men are dead and 15 seriously injured, some of them still in ICU,” he said. Two Camps, Competing Accusations The Uduere violence has produced sharply conflicting accounts from Egbo and Omo-Agege. Egbo, who hails from the community, accused Omo-Agege and his entourage of instigating the violence. He claimed two of his associates, Prince Oharisi and a man identified simply as Oche, were shot dead as Omo-Agege was concluding his campaign activities. Egbo alleged that Omo-Agege arrived after APC members had secured the town hall for a ceremony. “He came there and started abusing everybody, according to what I was told, saying I was his PA, I was his boy, and all of that,” he said. He further alleged: “On his way out, he ordered one of his boys, Efemena Umukoro, Akhima, one of the NDC key mobilisers who lost his life in the melee, to open fire on our people.” Egbo also said the community’s President-General, Cosmos Ejovwoke, was attacked and killed. “I found out that they clubbed and shot the President-General of the community,” he said. He demanded investigation by the Inspector-General of Police, declaring: “You come to my community to kill my President-General, killing my people, and you don’t even feel any remorse? We must do something about it. If we continue like this, then our democracy is in danger.” Omo-Agege, however, accused Egbo and his alleged political backers of orchestrating the attack. He listed four members of his campaign organisation as dead, including former Federal Character Commissioner, Moses Anaughe, while about 15 others sustained critical injuries. He questioned why the violence occurred despite the deployment of policemen. “We went to the campaign with full expectations, that with six trucks of policemen deployed to that venue to protect us in that event, we expected protection for everybody in that venue,” he said. “It never occurred to us that they (police) were merely coming to watch me principally executed.” He added: “There is no way you have close to 50 policemen in a venue and a minute after commencement of the attack, all of them ran away and left only you there.” Survivors’ Accounts Of Blood And Bullets One of the most harrowing accounts came from Chief Evans Ivwurie, Chairman of Omo-Agege’s campaign organisation, who was shot during the violence. Ivwurie alleged that the atmosphere became tense as the rival political gatherings proceeded, adding he personally complained to police officers about gunfire from the opposing gathering. “The Policemen told me they (APC supporters) were not shooting guns, that they were shooting knockouts (fireworks). I said but you can see them brandishing pump actions openly, shooting it,” he recounted. He alleged that violence erupted while Omo-Agege was addressing the campaign. “These APC thugs led by Egbo, the LG Chairman, started throwing stones at the direction of Omo-Agege and our people gathered there. They ended throwing the stones and all of a sudden they started shooting.” As people fled, he said, he tried to establish whether Omo-Agege was safe, alleging a man identified as Gueke, chairman of Ughelli Motor Parks, shot him in the head. “Immediately he saw me at a close range, he just shot at me, on my head. The bullet was so heavy, I fell flat to the ground without any energy,” he said. He further alleged that the gunman shot Anaughe twice in the chest. Another victim, Agbah, who had earlier been affected by the council’s action following his October rally, was shot in the neck. item.title: How Tinubu fought Obasanjo to reclaim Lagos coastline – Fashola
item.description: By Juliet Umeh As the 2027 general elections draw closer, political defections, shifting alliances and questions about leadership are beginning to shape the debate over who should govern Nigeria for another four years. But for former Lagos State Governor, Mr Babatunde Fashola, one important test for anyone seeking to lead the country is the ability to build relationships, work with others and remain committed to a political team, even in difficult times. Fashola believes President Bola Tinubu has demonstrated these qualities, arguing that his ability to retain political associates and bring former opponents into his camp makes him better placed to manage Nigeria’s diversity. In a pointed challenge to opposition leaders, the former governor asked voters to examine what happened to the people who worked with other presidential contenders and why many of them were no longer in their political camps. Fashola believes President Bola Tinubu has demonstrated these qualities, arguing that his ability to retain political associates and bring former opponents into his camp makes him better placed to manage Nigeria’s diversity. In a pointed challenge to opposition leaders, the former governor asked voters to examine what happened to the people who worked with other presidential contenders and why many of them were no longer in their political camps. Speaking during an interview on Arise Television, Fashola said political relationships should serve as a reference point for assessing the leadership capacity of those seeking the presidency. “Where are all the people who worked with them today? That’s a job reference question. For those who want to vote, where are all the people who worked with these people? Why is it only President Tinubu that has all those who worked with him when he was governor still with him? And they were with him for 16 years or so, out of office, when he wasn’t a president,” he said. According to him, the ability to work with people is essential for anyone entrusted with managing a country as diverse as Nigeria. “If you are going to get entrusted with managing Nigeria’s diverse family, you must be able to work in a team. And you don’t just get up and jump away when there’s a crisis in the fold,” he said. Fashola noted that Tinubu remained in the All Progressives Congress, APC, despite internal disagreements, while some political leaders had abandoned parties that helped build their political careers. He also pointed to Tinubu’s ability to bring former opponents into his political fold, describing it as evidence of his capacity to build relationships across political divides. “Not just those who worked with him before, those who opposed him are now working with him. That’s how he has built a coalition of 30 state governors from one state, from Lagos. And that is profound, whether you like him or not,” he said. Why I refused to join another party Fashola’s argument about political loyalty also reflects his own experience as Lagos governor, when he said he resisted pressure to abandon his political platform in exchange for certain benefits from the Federal Government. He recalled that during a meeting with a former President, an unnamed governor suggested that Lagos would only regain access to Lagos House, Marina, if he joined the ruling party at the time. Fashola said he rejected the condition, insisting that political conviction should not be traded for government privileges. “I said, look, Mr President, if that is the condition, keep the house. And as long as I am alive, I won’t join your party. If unfortunately I die, and they bring my body into your party, I’ll wake up,” he recalled. He said his administration also faced disagreements with the Federal Government over issues including approval for the proposed Lekki Port and access to funds belonging to Lagos State. How Tinubu fought Obasanjo over Lagos coastline Fashola also defended Tinubu’s claim that he played a major role in efforts to protect the Lagos coastline from the Atlantic Ocean, particularly around Victoria Island. He recalled that the Federal Government had spent about N4 billion pumping sand to protect the coastline, but erosion continued to threaten properties and infrastructure. According to him, Tinubu repeatedly wrote to former President Olusegun Obasanjo seeking approval for a lasting solution, but the requests were initially rejected. Fashola, who served as Tinubu’s Chief of Staff at the time, said he personally drafted several of the letters. “I drafted those letters on his instructions to President Obasanjo every time. President Obasanjo would reply, no. The last one, I think it was something like, almost like, look, get out of my life, I will find a copy of the letter. I still have it in my records,” he said. He said about seven letters were written, with Tinubu insisting that the administration should continue pressing for approval. “Nobody should take the credit away from him. I was his Chief of Staff,” Fashola said, maintaining that Tinubu deserved recognition for the initiative. Certificate controversy, foreign trips On the controversy surrounding Tinubu’s academic records, Fashola described the debate as a distraction from pressing national issues, arguing that attention should instead be focused on the cost of living, fuel prices, employment, education and security. “How does this (controversy on certificate) reduce the cost of living crisis? No, how does that reduce the cost of fuel? How does it reduce their travel time? How does it pay their children’s school fees, which NELFUND does? How does it create jobs?” he asked. He also defended the President’s foreign trips, while acknowledging that Nigerians had the right to demand explanations about public spending. “Nigerians are entitled to ask questions about their president’s utilisation of the time and resources,” he said. However, he challenged opposition parties to go beyond criticising the administration and present practical alternatives to its policies. He argued that international engagements could support investment, infrastructure development and service delivery. Following the discharge and acquittal of the six men charged over the case in 2014, Fashola expressed sympathy with the Williams family, describing the late politician as a peaceful man and an outstanding public servant. “Funsho Williams was a man of peace, a fine gentleman, an outstanding public servant. No one deserved to be treated the way he was cruelly murdered,” he said. He said the case demonstrated the need for more effective police investigations and the use of forensic tools, including DNA analysis and fingerprint evidence, to identify suspects and secure convictions. Fashola also called for the prosecution of sponsors of electoral violence, arguing that holding prominent offenders accountable could discourage others. He, however, opposed the ‘rig and die’ slogan for election riggers, insisting that punishment must follow the law and respect due process. He recalled that more than 11 million Nigerians were connected to electricity during his four years as Minister of Power, adding that his administration pursued incremental improvements towards stable and uninterrupted supply. Fashola also welcomed the decentralisation of the power sector, saying greater participation by state governments could attract investment and introduce new solutions. Asked whether he would consider another political contest, he suggested that his time in public office had run its course. “I’ve run as hard as I can. So it’s time to stop running. It was a very humbling privilege to have served my country. I don’t take that for granted,” he said. Reflecting on the painful history of the Igbo, including the 1966 pogroms, displacement and civil war, she said Ojukwu’s memorial should inspire a commitment to ensuring that such tragedies never happen again. She called on traditional rulers to provide moral leadership, political leaders to rise above personal interests, and businessmen and women to invest in the homeland, while urging young people to channel their energies into innovation, enterprise and productive ventures. The minister also cautioned Igbo youths in the diaspora against the pursuit of illicit wealth, warning that criminal activities had brought disgrace to the people and landed some young people in detention rather than helping them build meaningful futures. She urged them to become worthy ambassadors of Igbo culture and contribute to creating a homeland where businesses could thrive, investors could operate confidently and families could celebrate festivities without fear. Bianca lamented the insecurity and economic difficulties in parts of the South-East, saying the region could not attract investment or encourage its people in the diaspora to return home if communities remained unsafe, businesses shut down and streets deserted. “Our land must once again become a place where our children are excited to return,” she said, stressing the need to restore confidence in the region’s business and investment climate She said Ojukwu’s ideals would only endure when they were translated into practical actions by those who inherited his legacy, noting that annual memorials alone could not adequately preserve the values of a great leader. Uwazurike demands Nnamdi Kanu’s release Meanwhile, Uwazurike renewed his call for the release of detained Biafra agitator, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu, insisting that he had committed no offence deserving of his continued detention. The MASSOB founder compared Kanu’s situation with that of Yoruba agitator, Sunday Igboho, who he said had been released, arguing that the difference in their circumstances was political. “Where is Sunday Igboho? Kanu didn’t commit any offence that is bigger or more sinister than that of Igboho. The only difference is that Sunday Igboho has a brother that is presently the President of Nigeria,” Uwazurike said. He added that Kanu would have been released if Peter Obi were Nigeria’s President. Uwazurike, who advocated non-violent agitation for Biafra, cautioned youths against resorting to violence, saying many had misunderstood the principles of self-determination and allowed social media narratives to distort the struggle. He urged the younger generation to embrace peaceful advocacy, insisting that violence was incompatible with the pursuit of self-determination. “I urge the new generation of indigenous people to abide by the principles of non-violence,” he said, citing Mahatma Gandhi as his inspiration. Uwazurike said he had no regrets over the sacrifices he made in the course of the Biafra struggle, including persecution and the destruction of his residence, insisting he was prepared to make even greater sacrifices if the quest could be achieved through peaceful means. “I want to even sacrifice more if Biafra could be actualised through non-violence,” he said, warning that violence would only undermine the struggle. He dismissed the absence of political elites at the event, saying the memorial was primarily about the people and not politicians, whom he accused of being divided by personal interests. He urged Ndigbo to preserve unity, which he described as one of Ojukwu’s enduring legacies. The event featured cultural displays, masquerades, a march-past by delegations from states in the old Eastern Region, lectures and goodwill messages. item.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, will today run a nationwide mock accreditation and result transmission exercise in all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), about seven weeks before the 2027 general election. He said the exercise would put the Commission’s new equipment and result systems under live conditions. “While this exercise allows INEC to stress-test our upgraded BVAS devices and verify our stricter INEC Result Viewing Portal, IReV, v,lidation safeguards—which automatically block arithmetic inconsistencies and over-voting, it also serves as an essential live dry run for our security architecture,” he said. The presidential and National Assembly elections hold on 16 January 2027 across 177,299 polling units, with governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections to follow on 6 February 2027. Amupitan said the Commission had procured new accreditation machines and set a lower voter threshold for the actual election in January. “INEC will deploy over 1.41 million ad hoc personnel alongside 57,000 newly procured Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) devices, calibrated at a reduced threshold of 850 voters per machine,” he said. He told the gathering that the rehearsal was as much a test of coordination with security agencies as of technology. “Strategy without rehearsal is merely aspiration,” he said. The INEC chairman called on the Commission’s Resident Electoral Commissioners and the Commissioners of Police in the states to take part fully. “I urge all Resident Electoral Commissioners and Commissioners of Police to treat November 28 as a full-scale operational rehearsal: test your communication lines, evaluate rapid-response times around mock polling centres, and identify any logistical or security blind spots while there is still ample time to resolve them,” he said. INEC had earlier published the list of polling units selected for the nationwide mock accreditation exercise, naming 17,656 locations across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory FCT. She said the situation became more dangerous when other passengers struggling under water began dragging her, forcing her to fight to free herself. She added, “When the incident happened, I told my son to remain calm and follow my instructions so that we would not perish. I know how to swim, so I was guiding him. “Suddenly, people who were trapped and struggling under the water started dragging me. I saw a bag floating and grabbed it, then gave it to my son to hold so he could stay afloat. “I had to bite the hands of those holding me underwater before they released me. I continued swimming until I was able to reach the shore. At a point, I became exhausted, but by God’s grace, I survived. “When I got to the shore and looked back into the river, I saw many people drowning. Most of them were children between the ages of two and eight, screaming for help. The children were the biggest casualties.” Silas also accused some youths who arrived from a neighbouring community of abandoning the rescue effort to fight over and steal the belongings of victims. She said she called their attention to the people drowning but they allegedly refused to help. “By the grace of God, I survived with all my children and other members of my family,” she added. ‘I LOST SEVEN FAMILY MEMBERS’ For Dr Timi Austin, the tragedy has left a painful family loss that he said would be difficult to overcome. He blamed the state government and the relevant maritime authorities for what he described as a failure to enforce safety regulations on the waterways. According to him, the absence of proper monitoring, passenger manifests and emergency response arrangements contributed to the tragedy. He said, “If you are to measure how I feel, I believe there will be no proper measurement for what I am going through because I am deeply pained. Some people whose family members travelled from Delta State, Lagos, Port Harcourt and other places do not even know the whereabouts of their loved ones. “Some people may still be thinking that their family members are somewhere, without knowing whether they are alive or dead. What are the authorities going to do about such people?” Austin said his wife and daughter were initially expected to be part of the journey, but his wife changed her mind at the last minute while they were at the waterfront. item.description: Four years ago, when Bola Ahmed Tinubu visited Enugu as a presidential candidate, he confronted a crowd that appeared less than enthusiastic about his ambition with a warning that has since acquired an enduring political significance. If they refused to support him and he eventually became president, he suggested, they might have to make do with a slice of bread soaked in water. It may have been intended as political banter, but the message was not lost on the people of the South-East. While constitutional requirements for ministerial representation are being met, the disparity raises legitimate questions about the spirit of federal character and the extent to which every region enjoys a sense of belonging in the federation. Curiously, some supporters of Tinubu in the South-East insist that the region has never had it so good in terms of appointments, access and federal patronage. Their position deserves consideration, but it does not erase the wider perception that the region remains inadequately represented in the distribution of political opportunities. There is also the question of electoral calculation. Before the 2023 election, Tinubu’s political strategy appeared to depend heavily on consolidating support in the South-West and making significant gains in the North. The political landscape has since changed. His administration is facing growing discontent in parts of the North, while the economic consequences of its policies have generated opposition across the country. Against this background, the President’s renewed courtship of the South-East appears to carry greater political significance. His meeting with Igbo residents in Lagos last Monday was particularly revealing. The atmosphere was warm and enthusiastic. Unlike the stern warning of four years ago, Tinubu was relaxed and playful, even reminding his audience of how they had disappointed him in 2023. He was referring to his defeat by Peter Obi in Lagos during the presidential election. Unfortunately, the President and some of his political associates appear not to have properly understood the reasons behind that electoral outcome. Rather than recognise the democratic choices of Lagos residents, some resorted to an ethnic interpretation that deepened divisions. One of the most unfortunate reactions came from Bayo Onanuga, then a spokesman for Tinubu’s presidential campaign and now a presidential spokesman. Shortly after the 2023 election, he issued a controversial warning to Igbo residents in Lagos, accusing them of interfering in the state’s politics. In his tweet, he declared: “Let 2023 be the last time of Igbo interference in Lagos politics. Let there be no repeat in 2027. Lagos is like Anambra, Imo, any Nigerian state. It is not No Man’s Land, not Federal Capital Territory. It is Yoruba land. Mind your business.” That statement was deeply troubling. It suggested that the political rights of Nigerian citizens could be restricted by their ethnic origins or ancestry. Lagos, like every other Nigerian state, belongs to all Nigerians who live, work and participate in its development. No ethnic group has an exclusive constitutional right to determine how other Nigerians should vote. Onanuga’s diagnosis was also defective. Tinubu’s defeat in Lagos was not the product of an Igbo conspiracy. He faced opposition from different political tendencies, including influential Yoruba figures. Afenifere, the prominent Yoruba socio-cultural organisation, endorsed Peter Obi in the 2023 presidential election. The Labour Party’s Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour also mounted a serious challenge to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu. Reducing these political developments to ethnic interference was therefore an attempt to avoid the more important questions about voter preferences, political dissatisfaction and the right of citizens to make independent electoral choices. What makes the episode particularly disappointing is the inclusive political reputation Tinubu built before becoming President. He popularised the appointment of non-indigenes into prominent positions in Lagos and demonstrated an ability to accommodate people from different ethnic backgrounds. He also facilitated the emergence of Joe Igbokwe, an Igbo man, as a prominent voice in the ruling political structure in Lagos. His own family connections reflect Nigeria’s diversity, with his son, Seyi, married to a woman of Igbo ancestry. It is against this background that the President must be careful about remarks that suggest lingering resentment over how the South-East or Igbo voters exercised their democratic rights in 2023. When Tinubu reminds the Igbo that they disappointed him at the polls, he risks reducing the relationship between the presidency and an entire region to electoral gratitude and punishment. That is not the essence of democratic leadership. The South-East does not need bread soaked in water, whether as a joke or a political metaphor. It needs infrastructure, industrial investment, federal appointments that reflect its place in the federation and equal opportunities for its citizens. Above all, it needs a President who recognises that no Nigerian should be made to feel like a second-class citizen because of where they come from or whom they voted for. Tinubu has an opportunity to correct the unfortunate impressions created by some of the rhetoric surrounding his emergence. His recent engagement with Igbo residents in Lagos was a welcome departure from the divisive exchanges of 2023. But warm words and political banter must translate into concrete action. The President should not be preoccupied with how the Igbo voted in 2023. He should be concerned about how Nigerians across all regions will assess his performance in 2027. Nigeria wants the Tinubu who embraces every community, irrespective of colour, creed, culture or political preference. The presidency is not a reward for those who voted for the winner, nor a punishment for those who chose otherwise. It is a national trust. Tinubu must govern as President of all Nigerians, not merely those who supported his ambition. If it was important before, it is now even more so because it is the road that now links commuters in that axis to the Coastal Road. Traffic has understandably, become heavier on the road. And probably because of this, especially during peak periods, another U-turn was very recently created that was probably not in the original design. This U-turn makes access to the Coastal Road easier and faster. It is unfortunately from the creation of this U-turn that the disintegration of the road started. Something that held the interlocking blocks together must have chipped off when the U-turn was created. As usual, it started with just one or two loose blocks. At this stage, a cup of mixed cement would have done the job. It would have been a stitch in time. But nothing was done. It became wider over the weeks as block after block were loosened. Soon, it became difficult for heavy duty trucks to do a U-turn without their tyres screeching. Then, it became obvious that smaller cars were trying to avoid the damaged area. But the damaged area was getting wider and soon became more and more difficult to avoid. Then, it threatened to cut one side of the road in two. A couple of days ago, I passed the road to find that a part of the U-turn had been sealed off for repairs. Thank God! Hopefully, the discomfort of regular commuters would be over soon. The wonder though, as always, is why things have to deteriorate before being fixed. Why we have to wait for a torn garment to need more than a dozen stitches to fix when a stitch in time would have saved the day and the embarrassment. Or why a simple repair work has to deteriorate in order to justify the award of a new contract. The Alternative Road is a busy road. Not only in terms of traffic, but also in terms of personnel. Government officials of different hues visit the road for one reason or the other. Even a bird would be challenged and accosted quickly if it perched wrongly along the road. It is therefore, hard to believe that the arm of government responsible for minor road repairs was not, until now, aware of this damage. It is hard to believe that the vigilance of government officials is only limited to perceived misdemeanors by the public and blind to things that need to be put right for the comfort of citizens and ease of governance. Government officials are quick to attack illegal structures and slow to repair damaged structures. The tale of the gradual dislodgement of interlocking blocks on this road, is in a way for me, a metaphor for the state of our national life. We tend to turn a blind eye to things until they get irredeemably wrong. The colossal sums we have spent on insecurity for example, could have been better spent elsewhere if things had been nipped in the bud. Instead, some northern politicians saw ‘Boko Haram’, its progenitor, as a card to be used against a Southern Christian President. The four national refineries would still be functioning today if leaders, starting from the military, saw them as national priorities instead of cash cows to be milked from time to time. Now, they are almost like scraps because the necessary stitching was not done as at when due. The proliferation of fake products is another issue. Fake products would not be this pervasive if concerned officials had acted swiftly to nip things in the bud. The list is endless. And together, they have made our national pathway to prosperity almost impassable. The second lesson, especially in this electioneering season, is that interlocking blocks are strong when held together just as unity gives a nation strength. Yet, we have politicians who are currently playing up ethnic and religious divisions for catchment votes. They play up weaknesses and fault lines. These leaders will rather see things damaged than repaired. They will rather see them destroyed than nurtured. They will rather weaken than strengthen. In fact, they delight in pointing out the loosened blocks in our national life. Their incessant attacks on the nation’s psyche are worse than the benign neglect of that road in Oniru, Victoria Island. He assured residents that the government he and his running mate, Senator Rabiu Kwankwaso, were seeking to form would unite the country and transform its economic and social sectors. The former Anambra State governor said the presidency required energy and commitment, arguing that it should not be treated as a retirement home. “Tinubu has failed to fulfil all his promises, including the restoration of the power sector. We will generate, transmit and distribute at least 10,000MW. Any money we borrow must be for investment. “The presidency requires energy; it is not a retirement home. We are tired of Tinubu’s government. Tinubu must go for a better Nigeria to emerge,” he said. Obi said his proposed administration would prioritise national unity, recalling that Nigeria had previously enjoyed stronger bonds across its different regions. “Let me assure you that the government Kwankwaso and I are seeking to form will unite Nigeria. Yesterday, I was in Minna, and I told them that Nigeria used to be united. No wonder Nnamdi Azikiwe and Chukwuemeka Ojukwu were born in Zungeru. We are going to reunite Nigeria. “The Nigeria we want is one where a child of nobody can become somebody,” he said. He also criticised the Federal Government’s borrowing, alleging that the Tinubu administration had borrowed more than previous administrations combined without commensurate visible results. According to him, his proposed government would focus on production, job creation and economic prosperity rather than continued dependence on consumption. “Kwankwaso and I want to form a government that will not give you excuses. We are going to form a government that will bring prosperity and production back to Nigeria. We will remove this country from consumption to production. “We already know the excuses, and we will tackle the challenges. Our government will demonstrate compassion, commitment and the zeal to get the job done,” he said. On corruption, Obi pledged that his administration would ensure public funds were deployed for the benefit of Nigerians. He questioned the utilisation of government loans, contrasting current borrowing with previous investments in major infrastructure projects such as the Kainji Dam. Obi further claimed that the number of Nigerians living in poverty had increased from 87 million when Tinubu assumed office to more than 140 million. He also expressed concern over youth unemployment, promising increased investment in education and healthcare if elected. Turning to the economy of Abia State, the NDC candidate promised to transform Aba, the state’s commercial centre, into an export hub and link it with Port Harcourt to establish a new economic corridor within the first few years of his administration. He also pledged to address the country’s security challenges, particularly the abduction of schoolchildren. “We cannot be in government while schoolchildren are being kidnapped and others taken into the bush. item.title: Manhunt launched for killers of NSCDC officer in Benue
item.description: By Peter Duru, Makurdi The Chairman of Agatu Local Government Area of Benue State, Mr Melvin Ejeh, has vowed to ensure the arrest and prosecution of those responsible for the killing of an officer of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), Inspector Anyebe Anya. Anya was reportedly killed by armed men who attacked him at his duty post at a checkpoint in Agatu a few days ago. The assailants were also said to have carted away his service rifle after the attack. Ejeh gave the assurance when he visited the deceased officer’s family in Otukpo to commiserate with them, describing Anya as a hardworking, honest and dedicated officer. He vowed that those behind the killing would not escape justice, assuring the bereaved family that efforts were already underway to track down and apprehend the perpetrators. “Those that killed him will not go unpunished. We will get all of them. I knew him personally. He was a very hardworking, honest man who was committed to his work. “The whole community is mourning his death. The people of Agatu are shocked and grieving over his death. “We console his family. He was a committed officer. I can assure you that we will get those involved and they will be brought to justice. There is a hunt for them already. “The entire Agatu people will not rest until he gets justice, that I can assure his family,” the chairman said. Efforts to reach the Public Relations Officer of the Benue State NSCDC Command, SC Michael Ejelikwu, for comments were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report. item.title: Meet Emmanuel Emegha, Chelsea’s new striking sensation who has Nigerian roots
item.description: By Enitan Abdultawab Chelsea’s latest attacking prospect, Emmanuel Emegha, is already giving supporters reasons to pay attention after scoring against Nottingham Forest on Friday. While the Blues trailed by two goals to nil, the 23-year-old striker, who joined Chelsea from French side Strasbourg, came off the bench to replace Danny Welbeck, found the net in the 54th and 89th minutes, and offered the Blues a lifeline in their Premier League encounter. However, his goals were not enough as Forest held unto their lead after Morgan Gibss-White had extended it immediately after, bringing the game to a 3-2 full-time result. Before the Forest clash, Emegha put Chelsea ahead at home when they hosted Leeds United last week. Unfortunately, he could not save the team from capitulating to a 1-4 defeat in the game. But beyond his growing reputation in England, Emegha has an interesting connection to Nigeria. Born in The Hague, Netherlands, to a Togolese father and a Nigerian mother, the powerful forward has West African roots. His Nigerian heritage makes him a player of interest to Nigerian football fans, particularly those following the growing number of players of Nigerian descent making waves in European football. However, Emegha has chosen to represent the Netherlands internationally. He made his senior debut against Poland in November 2025, explaining that the Netherlands is his country and that he is proud to be Dutch. Although Nigeria missed out on having him represent the Super Eagles, his progress at Chelsea gives Nigerian fans another reason to follow his career closely. At 23, Emegha has the physical presence, pace and goalscoring instincts to make an impression in English football. His latest goals against Nottingham Forest are another early signs of what he could offer Chelsea. item.title: Chelsea beaten at Nottingham Forest as poor run continues
item.description: Nottingham Forest claimed a memorable 3-2 victory over Chelsea at the City Ground on Friday night, November 27, piling further pressure on Blues manager Xabi Alonso after another disappointing performance from his side. Forest made a flying start to the encounter, taking the lead just five minutes into the game through Igor Jesus, who produced a superb volley from Daniel Muñoz’s cross to put the hosts ahead. Chelsea struggled to find their rhythm in the opening half, with Forest looking more dangerous and organised in attack. Despite enjoying more possession, the visitors failed to turn their dominance on the ball into meaningful goalscoring opportunities. The hosts doubled their advantage shortly after the restart when Morgan Gibbs-White converted from the penalty spot in the 51st minute. The penalty was awarded after Wesley Fofana brought down Liam Delap inside the Chelsea box. However, Chelsea responded three minutes later through substitute Emmanuel Emegha, who pulled one back after Pedro Neto’s effort took a deflection and fell kindly into his path. The goal briefly offered Chelsea hope of mounting a comeback, but Forest remained dangerous and restored their two-goal cushion in the 72nd minute when Gibbs-White grabbed his second of the evening. Chelsea refused to surrender, with Emegha scoring again in the 89th minute to reduce the deficit to 3-2 and set up a tense finish. However, Forest held on through the closing moments to secure all three points and condemn Chelsea to another painful defeat. The result represents another setback for Alonso, whose team have struggled for consistency in recent weeks. Chelsea’s defensive weaknesses and inability to control crucial moments once again proved costly. For Nottingham Forest, the victory provides a significant boost and a valuable reward for their determination and attacking efficiency. Chelsea must now turn their attention to their next Premier League fixture against Crystal Palace as they look to recover from another frustrating night. item.title: A Weekend For Proof
item.description: INEC tests its systems on Saturday. Opposition leaders face their own test on Monday. Campaign violence makes both exercises more consequential. By Tuesday, Nigerians should have fresh evidence about two institutions seeking their confidence. INEC will have conducted its nationwide mock accreditation and result-upload exercise. Opposition parties will have had their scheduled opportunity to formalise cooperation in Abuja. The first must demonstrate operational readiness. The second must demonstrate an ability to act together. Both approach those tests amid a worsening concern: whether citizens can participate in the campaign safely. Wednesday’s attack on Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) supporters in Benin City, Edo State, confirmed by the police, followed Monday’s deadly violence in Delta. Edo police reported one person injured and ordered an investigation. The attackers’ political affiliations and any sponsors have not been established. That development changes the context of the coming days. Electoral preparation now requires visible progress on protection, accountability and public confidence alongside equipment and political agreements. Saturday: Let The Test Produce Evidence INEC’s mock exercise is scheduled for November 28, from 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Nigerian time, in 17,676 selected polling units. It will test accreditation, election devices, and the uploading and viewing of simulated results. Registered voters in the selected units are expected to participate. The most useful outcome would be a public account of performance. How many locations opened on time? How many participants were successfully accredited? Where did devices fail? How long did uploads take? How were exceptions resolved? A rehearsal can reveal problems that announcements cannot. Finding a fault early allows INEC to correct it. Explaining that correction gives citizens a reason to have greater confidence. The exercise also has practical support from state governments. Lagos has cancelled Saturday’s sanitation exercise, while Anambra has postponed its own, to avoid obstructing participation. Those decisions remove an immediate obstacle. The remaining test concerns delivery at the selected polling units. Monday: What Will Opposition Unity Require? Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, Seyi Makinde and other opposition leaders are expected at the November 30 summit. Their attendance and any signed commitments remain forthcoming. The APC says it is untroubled by the proposed gathering. The parties’ task is to define cooperation precisely. Joint election monitoring could be valuable. So could common procedures for documenting intimidation, sharing verified information and coordinating legal responses. Presidential cooperation presents more difficult choices. Supporters need to know whether their parties intend to campaign separately, endorse an existing candidate or pursue another lawful arrangement. A declaration of unity leaves those questions open unless it specifies obligations.

The summit should therefore be assessed through what participants authorise, who carries out the decisions and when implementation begins. Any agreement must reach state organisations, constituency candidates and polling agents to become electorally useful. Obi’s Campaign Faces An Organisational Dispute A fresh disagreement within the support-group environment complicates the NDC’s preparations. A group led by John Ughulu announced on Friday that it was withdrawing campaign and mobilisation support under the OK Movement name. The NDC rejected its claim to represent the authentic movement, while Obi’s spokesman said his campaign did not recognise Ughulu’s group as one of its support organisations. This establishes a dispute over authority and affiliation. It does not establish how many voters, organisers or functioning structures have changed allegiance. Its practical significance depends on identifiable capacity: people organising locally, maintaining campaign operations and preparing for election day. For Obi and Kwankwaso, the broader challenge is to coordinate their recognised organisations and give volunteers clear responsibilities. For anyone claiming to withdraw support, the test is whether the claimed structures can be independently demonstrated. Political labels alone cannot measure electoral strength. Separately, the House of Representatives called for investigations and action against perpetrators and sponsors. Its discussion of possible emergency measures was conditional; it did not declare a state of emergency. In Edo, the police account confirms an attack and a gunshot injury. The NDC alleges a broader pattern of political intimidation. The APC rejects allegations that it is coordinating attacks, and the Edo governor has denied government involvement. Those accusations and denials require examination against evidence. The immediate standard is equal protection. Campaign organisers need reliable security arrangements. Victims need care and access to justice. Investigators need to identify individual responsibility and any sponsorship. Repeated condemnation without visible investigative progress risks teaching citizens that intimidation carries little consequence. That perception can discourage participation even where no attack occurs. The Government’s Performance Remains On Trial Campaign disputes must leave room for scrutiny of governing choices. Atiku has questioned a reported decline in oil receipts, while Makinde’s campaign has challenged the relationship between expenditure plans and borrowing. The figures being debated concern an earlier reporting period; their renewed prominence does not make them newly incurred losses. For Tinubu’s administration, the response should explain revenue performance, spending priorities and what citizens receive from public expenditure. For challengers, criticism should lead to a credible alternative. Promises on security, jobs, electricity and education require resources. Voters deserve to understand the proposed trade-offs. The governing party seeks another mandate on its record and plans. The opposition seeks one on its diagnosis and proposed remedies. Both should face questions of cost, delivery and accountability. APC/Tinubu: The immediate test is whether the governing camp can combine its campaign strength with confidence in public institutions and equal protection for political competitors. ADC/Atiku: The leadership and nomination appeal remains consequential. The ADC has sought a stay of execution; the latest material reviewed does not establish that a stay has been granted. Its postponed Jigawa rally was attributed by a party spokesperson to mobilisation and logistical preparations, rather than a verified government prohibition. NDC/Obi–Kwankwaso: Campaign safety and coordination among support organisations require attention. The disputed OK Movement announcement cannot yet be translated into a quantified electoral loss. APM/Makinde and other opposition partners: Monday will test their willingness to accept defined responsibilities within a common arrangement. State contests: The Court of Appeal has reserved judgment in the dispute over Isa Pantami’s PDP governorship nomination in Gombe. A reserved judgment is a pending decision, rather than a victory for either side. Recent local and off-cycle elections remain useful indicators when turnout, competitiveness and local conditions are considered. They provide evidence about organisation and participation, without automatically predicting a presidential result. Election Watch assessment : The coming weekend offers measurable tests of readiness and cooperation. No fresh, credible polling reviewed for this edition establishes a national swing. item.title: Ogun 2027: Court dismisses Hunye’s suits against Adeola’s APC candidacy
item.description: …Adeola hails judgment …as Hunye heads to Court of Appeal By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Federal High Court sitting in Abeokuta, Ogun State, on Friday dismissed two suits filed by Hon. Abayomi Semako Hunye challenging the emergence of Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, as the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate for the 2027 election. Delivering judgment in the two consolidated suits, Justice Okeke held that the cases lacked merit and consequently dismissed them. The suits, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1127/2026 and FHC/AB/126/2026, were instituted by Hunye against the APC, Senator Adeola and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), challenging the process through which Adeola emerged as the party’s governorship candidate. Reacting to the judgment, Adeola commended the judiciary, describing the decision as a vindication of the rule of law and the judicial process. In a statement issued by his media adviser, Chief Kayode Odunaro, the senator expressed satisfaction with the outcome while appreciating his legal team for what he described as their painstaking efforts in defending the suits. Adeola said, “I want to commend the Honourable Justice for his erudite judgment in these cases challenging my overwhelming and widely accepted victory in our party primary. I also commend my legal team for the painstaking defense put up during the process. “This victory is yet another milestone in our quest for equity and justice in the Ogun State 2027 election. To God be the glory once again.” The senator said that despite the legal challenges, he had remained focused on consolidating support for his candidacy across the state through engagements with political stakeholders and other interest groups. He added that his engagements had also included the presentation of his nine-pillar ITESIWAJU Agenda, which he described as his development blueprint for Ogun State. According to him, the court’s decision would allow him to concentrate more fully on preparations for the 2027 governorship election and take his campaign message to voters across the state. Adeola also urged APC members and his supporters, irrespective of their political affiliations, to remain united and focused, stressing that his ambition was driven by a desire to serve the people and contribute to the development of Ogun State. However, Hunye has rejected the outcome of the proceedings and indicated his intention to appeal the judgment. item.content:encoded: …Adeola hails judgment …as Hunye heads to Court of Appeal By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Federal High Court sitting in Abeokuta, Ogun State, on Friday dismissed two suits filed by Hon. Abayomi Semako Hunye challenging the emergence of Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, as the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate for the 2027 election. Delivering judgment in the two consolidated suits, Justice Okeke held that the cases lacked merit and consequently dismissed them. The suits, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1127/2026 and FHC/AB/126/2026, were instituted by Hunye against the APC, Senator Adeola and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), challenging the process through which Adeola emerged as the party’s governorship candidate. Reacting to the judgment, Adeola commended the judiciary, describing the decision as a vindication of the rule of law and the judicial process. In a statement issued by his media adviser, Chief Kayode Odunaro, the senator expressed satisfaction with the outcome while appreciating his legal team for what he described as their painstaking efforts in defending the suits. Adeola said, “I want to commend the Honourable Justice for his erudite judgment in these cases challenging my overwhelming and widely accepted victory in our party primary. I also commend my legal team for the painstaking defense put up during the process. “This victory is yet another milestone in our quest for equity and justice in the Ogun State 2027 election. To God be the glory once again.” The senator said that despite the legal challenges, he had remained focused on consolidating support for his candidacy across the state through engagements with political stakeholders and other interest groups. We have faith in the appellate process and remain confident that, in time, truth and legality will prevail,” he said. item.title: Two Nigerians arrested over romance scam in Thailand
item.description: Two Nigerian men have been arrested in Thailand over their alleged links to an international romance scam network targeting victims across Southeast Asia. The suspects, aged 41 and 30, were arrested on November 18 at a condominium in Ban Mai, Pak Kret district, Nonthaburi, following an investigation by Thailand’s Immigration Division 3 and Provincial Police Region 1. According to local media outlet, The Thaiger, undercover police officers disguised themselves as food delivery workers to gain access to the suspects’ apartment. With the help of security guards, the officers approached the condominium and pretended to have a parcel for delivery. When one of the men opened the door, they identified themselves as police officers and moved in to arrest both suspects. A search of the apartment reportedly led to the recovery of laptops and mobile phones containing messages linked to fake online identities posing as US military personnel. Investigators suspect the identities were used to establish romantic relationships with potential victims as part of an international scam operation. Police also reportedly found social media accounts allegedly created to deceive Thai residents. The arrests followed an earlier investigation on November 12, when police detained another Nigerian man, aged 37, at Owl Market in Nonthaburi over suspected links to the same network. Investigators later searched a condominium in Bang Kraso, Mueang Nonthaburi, where suspected members of the group had reportedly stayed. However, the men had left before the search. Police subsequently traced the two suspects to another condominium in the Muang Thong Thani area, where they were believed to have stayed for two to three days before their arrest. The Thaiger reported that both men confessed during questioning. However, the charges publicly reported against them are immigration-related offences, including illegal entry and unauthorised residence. One of the suspects, aged 41, had reportedly overstayed his permitted stay in Thailand by 411 days. Authorities revoked their permission to remain in the country and transferred them to Pak Kret Police Station for further legal proceedings ahead of deportation. The investigation into the suspected romance scam network is ongoing. Thai police have not disclosed the identities of the alleged victims, the amount of money involved or the specific roles the two men allegedly played in the operation. The reported immigration charges do not amount to convictions for romance fraud. The post Two Nigerians arrested over romance scam in Thailand appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Adesua Etomi celebrates negative cancer test
item.description: Nollywood actress Adesua Etomi-Wellington has celebrated testing negative for cancer after months of medical procedures, hospital visits and uncertainty over her health. The actress announced the development on Friday in an Instagram video, expressing gratitude to God following the latest result from her medical tests. “The doctor just called me back with the result from the lab, no cancer… God is good,” she said. The video showed some of the medical procedures she underwent, while other pictures revealed bruises on her body and redness beneath one of her eyes. Etomi-Wellington also shared a video of friends and well-wishers celebrating the result with her. Reflecting on her experience, the actress described 2026 as one of the most difficult periods of her life, explaining that her reduced public appearances were linked to her health struggles. “2026 really tried it. I know I’ve been quieter than usual this year (and that’s saying something), but behind the silence were some of the most difficult months of my life,” she wrote. She disclosed that the ordeal involved several medical procedures, scans, injections and hospital visits, adding that she received treatment from medical teams in Nigeria and the United States. “This year threw everything at me, but by the grace of God, I am NOT EASILY BROKEN,” she added. The actress also expressed appreciation to her husband, singer and politician Bankole Wellington, popularly known as Banky W, their children, friends and family members for supporting her throughout the difficult period. “To my friends and family who prayed for me, stood in the gap and held me through some of my darkest days, I will never take your love for granted,” she wrote. The health update comes two days after the couple released a gospel song, On My Way , on November 25 to celebrate their ninth wedding anniversary. The track, credited to Etomi-Wellington, who performs under the musical name Susu, and Banky W, is the lead single from their forthcoming joint album, Not Easily Broken , expected in 2027. The actress described the song as “the soundtrack to our testimony and thanksgiving”, linking its message to their personal experiences. The couple have previously spoken about their health challenges. In May 2024, Banky W disclosed that he had undergone his fourth surgery for cancer after earlier procedures to remove cancerous tumours. Etomi-Wellington also revealed in March 2025 that she battled hyperemesis gravidarum, a severe form of pregnancy sickness, during her second pregnancy. The condition left her ill for months and required hospitalisation before she underwent an emergency Caesarean section. The post Adesua Etomi celebrates negative cancer test appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Osun LG Crisis Will Be Fully Resolved In The Next One Week — Gov Adeleke
item.description: Governor Ademola Adeleke has assured the people of Osun State that the protracted local government crisis in the state will be resolved within the next week, following President Bola Tinubu’s intervention. Governor Adeleke gave this assurance in his inaugural speech during his second-term inauguration held at Osogbo City Stadium, where he listed some of the priorities of his second-term administration across all sectors. “I am glad to announce that Mr President has intervened in the local government matter and in the next one week, the crisis will be fully resolved. Once this is done, our administration will ensure the rehabilitation of the remaining 102 primary health care centres,” he said. Osun Governor Ademola Adeleke was sworn in as governor for a second term on November 27, 2026. Photo: Femi Ojomo/Channels Television. As part of his priorities, the re-elected governor promised to set up the Osun State Electricity Regulatory Commission, as well as infrastructural expansion and recruitment of teachers and rehabilitation of schools, including reviving technical colleges. He also said that job and wealth creation will be at the heart of his second term. “We will establish a digital hub in each of our three senatorial districts. This is to drive job creation in the digital economy,” Adeleke said. “In education, we will recruit more teachers and speed up school rehabilitation. We will expand bursaries and scholarships, keep tuition affordable, tackle cultism, and revive our technical colleges.” In the health sector, he said about 70 per cent of existing primary health care centres were rehabilitated and equipped with solar and power facilities in his first term. “We upgraded and completed 232 out of 332 primary health care centres. Governor Adeleke gave this assurance in his inaugural speech during his second-term inauguration held at Osogbo City Stadium, where he listed some of the priorities of his second-term administration across all sectors. “I am glad to announce that Mr President has intervened in the local government matter and in the next one week, the crisis will be fully resolved.
